questions.q: Normal service after an incident may resume only when the affected area has been:
options: Inspected and certified safe by the responsible official
Vacant for one full hour
Photographed by the station staff
Announced on the public address system
questions.explain: Certification is the gate — resumption without a 'declared fit' is prohibited, however long the delay.

questions.q: The correct restoration sequence after an incident is:
options: Full timetable at once, systems tested later, report first
Passengers informed, full speed running, inspection next day
Area certified safe, systems restored and tested, trains repositioned, phased service resumption, passengers informed, report and debrief
Trains repositioned, area certified afterwards, systems tested last
questions.explain: Certify, restore and test, reposition, resume in phases, inform, then report — this order is itself a safety procedure.

questions.q: Which systems are restored and tested before normal running, as part of restoration?
options: Only the ticket vending machines
Signalling, power, Platform Screen Doors (PSD) and other station systems
Only the station lighting
Only the catering equipment
questions.explain: Every system the incident touched — signalling, power, Platform Screen Doors (PSD) and station systems — is restored and tested, not assumed.

questions.q: In the restoration flowchart, systems are restored in an order that begins with:
options: Station shops, then power, then signalling
Signalling before any power is restored in all cases
Passenger announcements before all systems
Power, then signalling, communications and station systems
questions.explain: Power feeds the rest — the flowchart restores power, signalling, communications and station systems in that order.

questions.q: The first train movements through a restored area are made:
options: At caution or restricted speed
At maximum line speed to test the repair
Only with officials on board for a week
Backwards, to check the track
questions.explain: First movements prove the area gently — speed returns only after the proof.

questions.q: Service after an incident usually resumes first as:
options: Double frequency to clear the backlog
A phased pattern — often reduced frequency first, then the full timetable
Only premium trains
Next day's timetable started early
questions.explain: Phased resumption is deliberate: a thinner service that actually runs beats a full timetable that collapses again.

questions.q: Why are trains 'repositioned' before the service can be rebuilt?
options: Trains must be washed before running again
Drivers prefer different trains after an incident
Repositioning is needed for the incident photograph
Incidents leave trains in the wrong places — they must be moved to where the timetable needs them
questions.explain: A timetable is trains in the right places at the right times — restoration puts them back there.

questions.q: Gaps in the rebuilt service are filled mainly by:
options: Asking passengers to wait until the next day
Running trains at double speed
Depot insertions and short-turn trains until the timetable becomes real again
Cancelling alternate stations
questions.explain: Spare trains from the depot and short-turns plug the holes while the pattern rebuilds.

questions.q: During every stage of restoration, passengers must be:
options: Told nothing until the full timetable returns
Kept informed — what is running, what is not, and what to expect next
Given only the technical fault details
Asked to check the next day's newspaper
questions.explain: Information runs alongside restoration — passengers plan their journeys from it.

questions.q: After restoration, the incident process is completed by:
options: The incident report, enquiry inputs and lessons learned
A celebration at the depot
Deleting the incident log
Refunding every ticket automatically
questions.explain: Report and lessons learned close the loop — today's restoration becomes tomorrow's prevention.

questions.q: Lessons learned from an incident feed into:
options: The staff leave register
The catering menu revision
Corrective And Preventive Action (CAPA) — changes that stop the same incident repeating
Nothing — they are filed and forgotten
questions.explain: Corrective And Preventive Action (CAPA) is where a debrief turns into changed procedures, training or equipment.

questions.q: A section was evacuated during an incident. Before trains run through it again, the essential confirmation is:
options: All tickets have been collected
The evacuation has been announced in the press
The trains have been cleaned
All passengers and staff are clear of the track and the area is certified safe
questions.explain: Clear-of-people plus certified safe — a section never reopens on assumption.

questions.q: The failed train that caused an incident is still standing in the section. Restoration of the line requires it to be:
options: Left there and timetabled around permanently
Moved clear to a depot or siding when safe, under Operations Control Centre (OCC) direction
Pushed into a tunnel cross-passage
Sold for scrap on the spot
questions.explain: The Operations Control Centre (OCC) directs the failed train's removal — the running line must be physically clear.

questions.q: A station that was evacuated reopens to passengers when:
options: The all-clear is given by the authorised command after checks and headcount
The first train arrives at its platform
Passengers waiting outside start entering
The station shutters are repaired
questions.explain: Station reopening follows the all-clear — a formal decision after accounting, not crowd pressure.

questions.q: Why is the full timetable NOT restored in one step even when everything is repaired?
options: The timetable office needs a day to print it
Passengers prefer fewer trains after an incident
Trains and crews are out of position and the system must prove stable — a phased build-up avoids a second collapse
Drivers are not allowed to work after incidents
questions.explain: Repair fixes machines; phasing fixes positions and proves stability — both are needed.

questions.q: During phased restoration, headway between trains will initially be:
options: Smaller than normal from the first train
Zero at all stations
Unchanged from the first minute
Larger than normal, shrinking as the service builds up
questions.explain: Wider gaps at first are the visible sign of a careful restoration.

questions.q: Who declares the affected signalling and power systems 'fit' for normal service?
options: The responsible engineer or controller for each system
The first train driver to use them
The station master alone for all systems
Any technician present at the site
questions.explain: Each system has its own fit declaration by its own responsible official — the Operations Control Centre (OCC) acts on those declarations.

questions.q: Passenger information during restoration should include, most importantly:
options: The names of the engineers who repaired the fault
Which services are running, expected frequency and any alternatives such as bus bridging
The cost of the damage
The full technical enquiry report
questions.explain: Passengers need usable facts — running services, frequency and alternatives — not engineering detail.

questions.q: A restored power section is brought back into service gradually mainly to:
options: Save money on the electricity bill
Give passengers time to board slowly
Avoid a second trip from a sudden full load
Test each train's horn
questions.explain: Gradual loading protects the recovery — a second failure would be worse than a slow first one.

questions.q: After a signalling failure, restoration steps up through:
options: Test movement at caution, then gradually back to normal headway
Immediate full-speed running
A week of manual working regardless
Only empty trains for a month
questions.explain: The test movement proves the repair; headway then builds step by step.

questions.q: The Operations Control Centre (OCC) coordinates restoration because:
options: Station staff are not allowed to help
Only control sees the whole picture — systems, train positions, crews and passenger information together
Restoration needs no coordination at all
The depot is closed during incidents
questions.explain: The Operations Control Centre (OCC) holds every thread of the recovery — that is why it directs the sequence.

questions.q: An incident ends at night with the service closed. Restoration planning should still:
options: Wait for the morning shift to think about it
Cancel the next day's services automatically
Leave trains wherever they stopped
Certify the area and systems, reposition trains, and have a phased plan ready for the first services
questions.explain: Overnight is restoration time — the morning peak should meet a certified railway, not yesterday's wreckage.

questions.q: Which is a sign that restoration has been rushed unsafely?
options: Trains running at normal speed through an area that has not been certified fit
Passengers being informed at each stage
A reduced-frequency service starting first
A test train running at caution
questions.explain: Speed before certification is the classic rushed-restoration trap — the gate exists to stop exactly this.

questions.q: Post-incident, staff involved in the incident are important to the debrief because:
options: They must be punished before restoration
Their leave must be cancelled
Their first-hand account builds the report, the enquiry inputs and the lessons learned
They alone decide the compensation
questions.explain: The people who were there hold the facts — the debrief collects them while memory is fresh.

questions.q: Restoration is truly complete when:
options: The first train moves again
The full timetable is running reliably, passengers are informed, and the report with lessons learned is completed
The incident leaves the news
The failed equipment is thrown away
questions.explain: Movement is only the middle of restoration — reliability, information and learning complete it.
